title: What languages do you speak?
goal: Speak formally with *usted*, talk about languages and jobs, and use the right article.
bekal: say what you do for a living
ask questions with the basic question words

dialogs.title: Diálogo — En la oficina de la escuela
dialogs.intro: Enrolling a new student. Because it's formal, the whole conversation uses *usted*.

lines.speaker: Secretaria:
lines.text: Buenos días. ¿De dónde es usted, señor Tanaka?
lines.id: Good morning. Where are you from, Mr. Tanaka?
lines.literal: good day. from where are you (polite), mister Tanaka?

lines.speaker: Sr. Tanaka:
lines.text: Soy japonés, de Osaka. Pero ahora vivo en México.
lines.id: I'm Japanese, from Osaka. But I live in Mexico now.
lines.literal: am Japanese, from Osaka. but now I-live in Mexico.

lines.speaker: Secretaria:
lines.id: And do you speak English too?

lines.speaker: Sr. Tanaka:
lines.text: Sí, hablo japonés, inglés y un poco de español.
lines.id: Yes, I speak Japanese, English and a little Spanish.
lines.literal: yes, I-speak Japanese, English and a little of Spanish.

lines.speaker: Secretaria:
lines.id: And your friend? Is she Japanese too?
lines.literal: and your friend(female)? she also is Japanese(female)?

lines.speaker: Sr. Tanaka:
lines.text: No, no es japonesa. Es coreana, de Seúl.
lines.id: No, she's not Japanese. She's Korean, from Seoul.
lines.literal: no, not is Japanese. is Korean, from Seoul.

lines.speaker: Sr. Tanaka:
lines.text: Trabaja en un hospital. Es médica.
lines.id: She works in a hospital. She's a doctor.
lines.literal: works in a hospital. is doctor(female).

lines.speaker: Secretaria:
lines.id: Perfect. And do you work or study?
lines.literal: perfect. and you (polite) work or study?

lines.speaker: Sr. Tanaka:
lines.text: Estudio español por la mañana y trabajo por la tarde.
lines.id: I study Spanish in the morning and work in the afternoon.
lines.literal: I-study Spanish in the morning and I-work in the afternoon.

notes: **Usted takes the *él / ella* verb form.** That's why *¿habla usted inglés?* uses *habla*, not *hablas*. If you slip and use the *tú* form with someone you should address formally, you'll still be understood — you'll just sound too familiar.
**Su** = "your" (polite), but also "his" or "her": *su amiga* can mean your friend or his/her friend. It is ambiguous, and Spanish leaves it that way — context decides.
**Languages without an article.** *Hablo español*, not *hablo el español*. The article only appears when the language is the subject of the sentence: *el español es fácil* ("Spanish is easy").
**Un poco de + noun.** Notice the *de*: *un poco de español*, *un poco de agua*. But before an adjective, the *de* disappears: *un poco cansado*.
**O = or**, except before a word starting with an *o* sound. There it becomes *u*: *siete u ocho* (seven or eight). The reason is purely sound — two *o*'s in a row blur together.
**Por la mañana / por la tarde / por la noche** = in the morning / in the afternoon / at night. These are the most common time markers, and they never change form.
**Jobs have gender too.** *médico / médica*, *enfermero / enfermera*, *abogado / abogada*. Some ending in -ista don't change: *el dentista / la dentista* — only the article changes.
**Bienvenido / bienvenida / bienvenidos.** The form follows whoever is being welcomed: one man *bienvenido*, one woman *bienvenida*, a group *bienvenidos*.

grammars.title: El, la, un, una — a noun never travels alone
body: Every Spanish noun has a gender, and its article has to match. There's no way around it: learn each noun **together with its article** from day one — not *hospital*, but *el hospital*.
after: You'll guess right about eight times out of ten: words ending in **-o** are usually masculine; words ending in **-a**, **-ción** or **-dad** are usually feminine. The rest must be memorized — and the exceptions that trip up beginners most: *el día* (day) is masculine despite its -a, *la mano* (hand) is feminine despite its -o.
Plurals are easy: after a vowel add **-s** (*libro → libros*), after a consonant add **-es** (*profesor → profesores*).

blocks.text: Every Spanish question word carries a ´ — that's what sets it apart from the same word without a question. Compare *¿qué?* (what?) with *que* (that, which).

blocks.title: Questions without a question word
items: A statement becomes a question just by adding question marks and a rising tone at the end: *Vives en Madrid.* → *¿Vives en Madrid?* No need for "do" or for switching the word order as in English.
Moving the subject after the verb is also common and sounds slightly more formal: *¿Vive usted en Madrid?*
A "yes" answer usually repeats the verb rather than stopping at *sí*: *—¿Hablas español? —Sí, hablo un poco.* A bare *sí* sounds cold.

blocks.text: Remember: jobs take no article. *Soy ingeniera*, not *soy una ingeniera*. The article only comes in when there's an extra description: *soy una ingeniera muy ocupada*.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make a correct Spanish sentence.

items: Hablo japonés, inglés y un poco de español.

answers: ¿De dónde eres? — Vivo en Barcelona. — Hablo un poco de español. — ¿En qué trabajas? — Ella no es japonesa.
I study Spanish in the morning. — And his friend? Is she Korean? — I work in a bookstore. — I speak Japanese, English and a little Spanish. — No problem.
wave: Go back to **Unit 2**, but make the whole dialogue polite: every *eres* becomes *es*, every *te llamas* becomes *se llama*.
